title: Why Companies Fail: What 50 Years of Data Tells Us
gist: BCG Henderson Institute's 50-year database of 30,000+ US-listed firms shows five-year delisting risk fell from ~40% (early 2000s) to ~18%, but because of a prescreened listed population, private-market migration and state/central-bank support rather than corporate resilience, and these conditions can reverse. Failure is driven by financing conditions, deregulation and IPO waves, not the GDP cycle, and varies sharply by firm age, size and sector-specific shock mechanism.

themes.theme: US delisting risk: halved but not rare

insights.claim: Five-year failure (delisting) risk for US-listed companies peaked at around 40% in the early 2000s and has fallen to roughly 18%, about the 1980 level, per BCG Henderson Institute data on 30,000+ firms from 1975 to 2025.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Baseline: about one in five listed US companies delists within five years, so listed-universe attrition is a structural drag for passive stock pickers and index constituents.
insights.locator: The rate at which US companies disappear

insights.claim: At an 18% five-year delisting rate, roughly a quarter of US listed companies delist over an average seven-year CEO tenure, meaning one in four CEOs should expect their company to end as a listed entity on their watch.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Management-tenure framing: governance and capital-allocation decisions should assume a meaningful probability of exit (bankruptcy, takeover or take-private) within one CEO's term.
insights.quote: one in four CEOs should expect to preside over the end of their company’s life as a listed entity
insights.locator: In other words: one in four CEOs

insights.claim: BCG's corporate failure metric counts any delisting from a US exchange (bankruptcy, acquisition, or take-private) as failure, because all end the current management mandate, even though acquisition at a premium is good for shareholders.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Read the headline failure rate as 'management mandate ends' risk, not shareholder loss; it blends takeover upside with bankruptcy downside.
insights.quote: being bought at a premium is a good day
insights.locator: To get to this number, we assembled

themes.theme: Why failure fell: environment, not resilience

insights.claim: The two-decade decline in US delisting rates was enabled by environmental changes (a smaller, prescreened listed population and state support for marginal firms), not by companies becoming intrinsically more resilient, and some of those conditions are now reversing.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Don't extrapolate low recent failure rates; the drivers are reversible, so tail risk in listed equities is understated by the last 20 years.
insights.quote: Firms did not get better at surviving; the environment got better at deferring failure.
insights.locator: Neither explanation has anything to do

insights.claim: After the dot-com bust and Sarbanes-Oxley (2002), higher regulatory, disclosure and litigation costs of being public deterred weaker firms from listing, so today's listed US companies clear a higher bar.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Public markets are a prescreened, older population; selection effects, not quality improvement, explain lower attrition.
insights.locator: The listed population is smaller and prescreened

insights.claim: The average age at which a US listed company fails rose from 29 years in 2000 to about 43 years today.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Evidence that the listed universe has aged and that the fragile young-firm phase has left public markets.
insights.locator: Our data corroborates it

insights.claim: Deeper private capital markets, opened up by deregulation, let risky ventures stay private longer, moving the most dangerous phase of corporate life off-exchange and outside public failure statistics.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Early-stage failure risk is now concentrated in private-market portfolios (VC, growth equity) rather than in listed equities.
insights.quote: the most dangerous phase of corporate life has moved off-exchange
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the most dangerous phase

insights.claim: Large-scale government and central bank intervention after the 2008 global financial crisis and during COVID-19, plus near-zero interest rates through the 2010s, kept leveraged and marginal firms financed and prevented shocks from becoming exit waves.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Higher-for-longer rates or less willingness to bail out would remove the support that suppressed delistings; watch leveraged small caps.
insights.locator: Governments and central banks kept the marginal firms alive

insights.claim: Tighter monetary policy pushes highly leveraged firms into default with a lag: after Volcker-era hikes drove real rates to near 9% in 1981, average US five-year failure risk rose about 11 percentage points through 1984.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Rate-hike cycles are a leading indicator for delistings via default; screen for leverage after sustained real-rate increases.
insights.locator: Money gets expensive

insights.claim: Financial deregulation that opens new funding channels fuels takeover waves: the 1979 freeing of pension capital, junk bonds and Savings and Loan liberalization enabled 1980s LBOs, when over half of junk bond issues were takeover related.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: New financing channels (today's analogue: private credit) can drive delistings through M&A and take-privates rather than bankruptcy.
insights.locator: Finance gets deregulated

insights.claim: Industry deregulation (Airline Deregulation Act 1978, AT&T breakup 1984, Riegle-Neal 1994, Telecommunications Act 1996) each produced a wave of consolidation and exits by removing entry barriers and price controls.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Deregulation of a sector is a signal to position for consolidation: takeover targets up, weak incumbents exit.
insights.locator: An industry gets deregulated

insights.claim: IPO waves add younger, smaller and more fragile firms to the listed population, and peaks in IPO activity reliably precede peaks in failure risk, as in 1986 and 1996-1997.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: A hot IPO window is a lagging warning sign for future delistings; IPO-cohort exposure carries elevated attrition risk.
insights.quote: Peaks in IPO activity reliably precede peaks in failure risk
insights.locator: The listing window opens

themes.theme: The economic cycle is not the signal

insights.claim: BCG found no meaningful relationship between GDP growth and US delisting rates, either as predictor or outcome, including with lagged series.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Recession forecasts are a poor guide to aggregate corporate exit risk; watch financing conditions and deregulation instead.
insights.quote: We find no meaningful relationship between the general economic cycle and the rate at which companies delist
insights.locator: Conspicuously absent from those conditions

insights.claim: Bankruptcies and acquisitions move against each other over the cycle, so aggregate delistings barely change: in the global financial crisis US annual bankruptcy rates rose from about 1.7% (2007) to 4.2% (2009) while the merger rate fell from about 7.3% to 2.9%.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Decompose exit risk by route: in downturns, credit risk rises while takeover premia vanish, so the mix matters more than the total.
insights.locator: The reason is that the two main exit routes

themes.theme: Age and size: deaveraging the risk

insights.claim: US listed company failure risk exceeds 25% over any five-year window until age 20 and falls steadily over the first five decades after founding, because young firms lack stable business models, crisis experience and stakeholder track records.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Young listed firms warrant a structural failure-risk discount regardless of sector.
insights.locator: Age reduces risk but only to a point

insights.claim: Corporate failure risk bottoms at roughly 13% over five years around ages 50 to 60 and stays there, since old firms face external shocks plus rigid processes, legacy costs and declining adaptability.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Old incumbents are not safe; a hard floor of about 13% five-year exit risk persists for century-old firms.
insights.quote: No amount of experience buys exemption from an external shock
insights.locator: Yet experience does not insulate

insights.claim: In 2025 the smallest revenue quartile of US listed firms (under $40 million) carries about 26% five-year failure risk versus about 8% for the largest (over $3.5 billion revenue).
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Size is a strong inverse risk factor; small-cap portfolios embed roughly 3x the delisting risk of large caps.
insights.locator: Split the population by revenue size

insights.claim: The failure-rate gap between the smallest and largest US revenue quartiles widens to 25 percentage points in crises versus 15 in calmer periods, because large firms have buffers, diversified revenue and, as in 2008, access to reopening corporate bond markets when bank lending dries up.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: In a credit crunch, overweight scale; small firms dependent on bank lending have nowhere to turn.
insights.quote: What matters most is when scale pays out.
insights.locator: What matters most is when scale pays out

insights.claim: Scale protection eventually turns into exposure for the largest companies as complexity becomes expensive to manage and regulators pay closer attention.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Mega-caps carry their own failure mode: complexity costs and regulatory scrutiny.
insights.locator: The smallest firms are most exposed

insights.claim: Over 50 years most US sectors show similar five-year failure risk (real estate and communication services about 26%), with consumer discretionary higher at about 31% due to elastic demand, and utilities the structural exception at about 11% thanks to regulation and inelastic demand.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Sector baseline matters less than expected; utilities are the only consistently low-attrition sector.
insights.locator: Your sector does not decide how risky you are

insights.claim: Sector failure rates diverge only when a shock hits a sector's specific economics, so sector determines which crisis mechanism can reach a company rather than its baseline risk.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Map holdings to shock mechanisms (cost of capital, commodity price, technological displacement) rather than relying on sector averages.
insights.quote: Your sector does not decide how risky you are but which crises reach you.
insights.locator: Sectors diverge when a shock is specific

insights.claim: The Volcker-era cost-of-capital shock hit businesses dependent on cheap money (debt-financed fixed assets, credit-bought demand) hardest: real estate's five-year failure rate rose from 11% to 36%.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: In a sharp rate shock, real estate and other debt-financed, asset-heavy models are the first casualties.
insights.locator: The Volcker era was a cost-of-capital shock

insights.claim: The mid-1980s oil price collapse roughly doubled the energy sector's five-year failure rate from about 21% to 41%, concentrating damage in firms whose revenue depends on the commodity price and whose capital cannot be repurposed.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Commodity-price crashes produce sector-specific failure waves in non-redeployable-asset producers.
insights.locator: The oil price collapse of the mid-1980s

insights.claim: The dot-com crisis was a technological displacement shock that raised communication services firms' failure rate from about 25% to 46%, hitting both the displaced industry and the infrastructure built to serve it.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: When a technology reprices an industry, both incumbents and the build-out infrastructure layer are at risk; relevant analogue for today's tech capex cycles.
insights.quote: When a technology reprices an industry, the damage lands in the industry being displaced and in the infrastructure built to serve it.
insights.locator: The dot-com crisis was a technological displacement shock

insights.claim: Corporate failure rates move when financial plumbing (rates, credit, deregulation) moves, and a quiet decade is no promise about the next; BCG declines to forecast and says quantified risk measures do not replace judgment.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Monitor financing conditions, not GDP, as the driver of corporate exit risk.
insights.quote: the failure rate moves when the financial plumbing does, and a quiet decade is not a promise about the next one
insights.locator: What half a century of data does support

insights.claim: Companies facing rising failure risk should build slack (cash, reserved low-cost debt capacity, diversified funding) before it is needed, price failure risk into large capital bets, and use crises to gain share from less prepared competitors.
insights.speaker: Ulrich Pidun
insights.so_what: Favor balance-sheet-strong firms that can act countercyclically; they gain advantage as weaker competitors fail.
insights.locator: If you conclude your own risk is rising
